FastAPI is a modern Python web framework used for building APIs quickly. It is built on top of Starlette for the web parts and Pydantic for data validation. One of its main advantages is automatic request validation: if a client sends data that does not match the expected shape, FastAPI returns a clear error before your function code even runs.

FastAPI automatically generates interactive API documentation. By default, this documentation is available at the /docs endpoint, which uses Swagger UI,

able at the /docs endpoint, which uses Swagger UI, and at /redoc, which uses ReDoc. This is generated directly from your route definitions and Pydantic models, so it always stays in sync with your actual code.

To define an endpoint in FastAPI, you write a normal Python function and decorate it with something like @app.get("/path") or @app.post("/path"). The function's type hints tell FastAPI what data to expect and what to return, and Pydantic models are commonly used to describe the shape of r

odels are commonly used to describe the shape of request and response bodies.

FastAPI applications are typically run using an ASGI server such as Uvicorn. A common command to start a FastAPI app during development is "uvicorn app.main:app --reload", where --reload automatically restarts the server whenever code changes are detected, which speeds up development.

tClient, which lets you send fake requests to your endpoints in tests without needing to run a real server. This makes it straightforward to reach high test coverage on API route logic.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is an approach that combines a retrieval system with a language model to produce answers grounded in external documents. Instead of relying only on what the model learned during training, RAG first searches a knowledge base for relevant information and then feeds that information to the model as context.

A typical RAG pipeline has three stages. First, documents are split into small chunks, usually a few hundred characters or tokens each, so that each chunk c

ed characters or tokens each, so that each chunk covers a focused piece of information. Second, each chunk is converted into a vector embedding using a model such as a Sentence Transformer. These embeddings are stored in a vector database like FAISS, Pinecone, or Chroma. Third, when a user asks a question, the question itself is embedded and compared against the stored chunk embeddings to find the most similar ones. These retrieved chunks are then passed to a large language model along with the

n passed to a large language model along with the original question, and the model generates an answer using that context.

The main benefit of RAG is that it reduces hallucination. Because the model is instructed to answer only from the retrieved context, it is less likely to invent facts that are not supported by any document. RAG also makes it possible to update the knowledge base without retraining the model. If a document changes, you simply re-index it, and the next query will retrieve the

re-index it, and the next query will retrieve the updated information.

FAISS, which stands for Facebook AI Similarity Search, is a library for efficient similarity search over dense vectors. It supports several index types. The simplest is a flat index, which performs an exact nearest-neighbor search by comparing the query vector against every stored vector. This is slower on very large datasets but is exact and simple to reason about, which makes it a good starting point for smaller projects.

Sentence Transformers are a family of models fine-tuned specifically to produce sentence-level and paragraph-level embeddings where semantically similar text ends up close together in vector space. The all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model is a popular lightweight choice because it produces 384-dimensional embeddings quickly while still capturing meaningful semantic relationships between sentences.

Retrieval quality is commonly measured using Recall@K, which

quality is commonly measured using Recall@K, which checks whether the correct or relevant chunk appears within the top K results returned by the retriever. A high Recall@5 means that for most questions, the right piece of information is present somewhere in the top five retrieved chunks, even if it is not always ranked first.
